fact: System Analysis is the systematic process of studying an existing or proposed system to understand its structure, functions, processes and interactions in order to identify problems, determine requirements, and recommend improvements or solutions
System analysis can also be defined as the process of understanding and specifying in detail what an information system should accomplish

System analysis is all about understanding the business and its goals and strategies, defining requirements for information systems that support those goals and strategies, and supporting the business

The purposes of system analysis are to ensure the system meets user and organisational needs, to reduce the risk of system failure, to provide a clear foundation for system design and development, and to improve efficiency, accuracy and decision-making within the organisation

System Design is the phase of system development that involves translating the requirements identified during system analysis into a detailed blueprint for building the system, defining how the system will be structured, how its components will interact, and how it will operate to meet specified functional and non-functional requirements
Systems Design specifies in detail how the many components of an information system should be physically implemented

A Systems Analyst is a professional who investigates, analyses and evaluates an organisation's information systems and business processes with the objective of designing or improving systems that effectively support organisational goals
The systems analyst acts as a link between business users and technical development teams, ensuring that business needs are accurately translated into technical specifications

The seven roles and responsibilities of a systems analyst are requirements analysis, system evaluation, feasibility studies, system modelling and documentation, the liaison role, solution recommendation, and support during development and implementation
Under feasibility studies the analyst assesses technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule feasibility of proposed systems
Under system modelling and documentation the analyst prepares models such as Data Flow Diagrams, Use Case Diagrams and Entity-Relationship Diagrams
A systems analyst is a business professional who uses analysis and design techniques to solve business problems using information technology; essentially a system analyst is a problem solver

To solve a problem the analyst must FIRST understand the problem and learn everything possible about it, including who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected by solving the problem
After understanding the problem the analyst must confirm with management that the benefits of solving the problem outweigh the costs

When defining requirements the analyst states what specific objectives must be satisfied, what data needs to be stored and used, what processing must be done to the data, and what outputs must be produced
What needs to be done must be defined first, and how it will be done is not important yet
Many different alternatives must be considered, and the challenge is to select the best, that is the solution with the fewest risks and most benefits
Systems design specifications describe the construction details of all system components, including databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces, and conversion plans

Building a system based on incomplete or misunderstood requirements may lead to over budgeting, late delivery, or delivery of a system that does not fully solve the problems it was intended to address

The analyst's approach to solving problems has eight steps in order: research and understand the problem; verify that the benefits of solving the problem outweigh the costs; define the requirements for solving the problem; develop a set of possible solutions (alternatives); decide which solution is best and make a recommendation; define the details of the chosen solution; implement the solution; monitor to make sure you obtain the desired results
A system is a collection of interrelated components that function together to achieve some outcome
An information system is a collection of interrelated components that collect, process, store and provide as output the information needed to complete business tasks

An information system can also be described as an arrangement of people, data, processes and information technology that interact to collect, process, store and provide as output the information needed to support an organisation
The purpose of an information system is to process input, maintain data, produce reports, handle queries, handle online transactions, and generate other outputs

A subsystem is a system that is part of another system, so subsystems are one way to think of a system's components; for example a sales management system might be a subsystem of a customer relationship management system
The approach of dividing a system into components, decomposing a system into subsystems which can be further decomposed, is called functional decomposition
Viewing a system as a collection of subsystems lets the analyst focus attention on a single area of a business, a group of related areas, or the interfaces among areas

A systems analyst requires a combination of technical, analytical and interpersonal skills, and needs to understand how to build information systems, the business they work for and how it uses each type of system, and people and the way they work
People are the source of requirements information, the labour that builds systems, and the ultimate users of the information system

The six fundamentals a systems analyst should understand are computers and how they work; file, database and storage hardware and software; input and output hardware and software; computer networks and protocols; programming languages, operating systems and utilities; and communication and collaboration technology such as digital telephones, videoconferencing and web-based document management systems
TOOLS are software products used to develop analysis and design specifications and completed system components, while TECHNIQUES are strategies for completing specific system development activities

The four types of tools used in system development are software packages such as Microsoft Access and Adobe Dreamweaver, integrated development environments such as Oracle JDeveloper and Microsoft Visual Studio, computer-aided visual modelling tools such as Rational XDE Modeller, Visible Analyst and Embarcadero Describe, and by extension the specifications they create, store, modify and manage
Examples of techniques include project planning, cost/benefit analysis, interviewing, requirements modelling, architectural design, network configuration, and database design techniques

Business knowledge means understanding business processes, organisational structures and industry practices so systems align with organisational goals, including what business functions organisations perform, how they are structured, how they are managed, and what type of work goes on in them
Specifics the analyst needs to know about a company are what the organisation does, what makes it successful, what its strategies and plans are, and what its traditions and values are

Interpersonal skills are the analyst's MOST IMPORTANT skills, because analysts rely on managers, users, programmers, technical specialists, customers and vendors to take a system from initial idea to final implementation

The analyst is a translator for all project participants, translating business objectives into functional requirements, user needs into system specifications, and technical jargon and details into terms non-technical personnel can easily understand
The analyst must be an effective communicator in many contexts, including conversations, interviews, technical reviews and formal presentations

Communication skills matter because the analyst must interact with users, managers and technical staff to gather requirements, explain system concepts and document specifications clearly, which prevents misunderstandings and ensures requirements accurately reflect user needs
